extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of ecclesiastical/architectural history
extracted.subtask_description: A historical and architectural survey of English cathedrals and 'Lady Chapels' from the Norman period through the 19th century, describing construction, damage, restorations, siting, function, and stylistic judgments. The text records conventions, exceptions, and examples across many dioceses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of design (continuous construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Salisbury Cathedral ... carried out from beginning to end with unbroken unity of purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous prosecution of work (commencing at the eastern end and advancing westward) produces a complete, unified example of English architecture; this unity is presented as a desirable attribute and contrasted with cathedrals built in stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural blending vs. unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Other cathedrals in England exhibit in almost every case a conglomerate of several orders of architecture, blended generally with great skill, but necessarily lacking to some extent in unity of design in consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blending multiple stylistic orders can be skillful, but it typically reduces overall unity of design — an implicit evaluative criterion when judging cathedral architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate style for ecclesiastical buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: However much more admirable the Gothic style may be admitted to be for ecclesiastical purposes, ... the grandeur of St. Paul's grows upon one the more familiar one becomes with it; and certainly no tower ... could possibly dominate a vast city like London in the way that Wren's splendid dome does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gothic is implicitly preferred for ecclesiastical purposes, but classical (as in Wren's St. Paul's) can be effective and appropriate in particular civic contexts; style-suitability should consider purpose and setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lady Chapel siting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is true that the Lady Chapel was generally erected at the extreme east end ... but the ecclesiastics and architects of the Middle Ages did not consider themselves bound by a hard and fast rule ... otherwise, the north aisle of the Church, or a convenient site near the Choir, was utilised for the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable locations include: extreme east end, east end of the choir/presbytery, north or south side of choir/nave, west end, over the chancel, over a porch, above a thoroughfare, connected to transept or chapter-house. The text gives many place-examples (Canterbury, Oxford, Bristol, Peterborough, Durham/Galilee exception, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical site selection (availability-driven placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It seems to have been built by the parishioners, and not by the abbot and convent, and its position is due to its occupying the only available spot, and where only two walls wanted building." (Waltham example.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ideal placement is impossible, chapels were sited pragmatically in the available space — a legitimate and common practice; parish foundations often took the only feasible spot rather than follow a strict rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founding purposes and functional criteria for Lady Chapels
rubrics_metrics.description: These buildings were generally founded not only to satisfy the spirit of the age, which demanded the veneration of the Mother of our Lord, but also to afford the necessary accommodation at the east end for the increased number of clergy. The founders, moreover, hoped to secure an augmentation of the revenues, by the offerings of the faithful ... The building, in many instances, became the depository of the relics of a saint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lady Chapels served multiple functions: devotional focus to the Virgin, extra liturgical space for clergy, chantry services and obits, repositories for relics, and mausolea/chantry-tombs. Founders expected both spiritual and material returns (offerings, endowments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding excess Marian cult / theological restraint in design
rubrics_metrics.description: English Churchmen, in their desire to honour the Mother of Christ, were careful to avoid this evil example [of Mariolatry] ... The erection of smaller buildings, and the setting apart ... of one of the side aisles rather than the sanctuary itself, tend to show that they did not assign to the Blessed Virgin that divine honour which was due only to her Son and Lord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and siting choices reflect theological caution: use separate/smaller chapels rather than converting principal sanctuary space to avoid elevating Marian cult above Christ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration and preservation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Something in the way of restoration was attempted in this century, but it was for the most part done ignorantly, and no small part of the restoration of the nineteenth century has consisted in undoing so far as possible the work of the eighteenth. ... the guardians of these treasures ... have for the most part been conscious of the greatness of their trust, and the fabrics have been dealt with reverently and with judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restorations should be undertaken with knowledge, reverence, and judgment; avoid ignorant or stylistically insensitive 'improvements' (criticized 18th-century work). Good modern restoration may involve undoing prior harmful interventions and restoring historic character (examples: Truro commencement, restorations at Bristol, Chichester, St. Albans, Peterborough).
